{{Short description|Lemma in cryptography}}
{{MOS|date=February 2023|reason=use of second person; see [[MOS:YOU]]}}

The '''leftover hash lemma''' is a [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] in [[cryptography]] first stated by [[Russell Impagliazzo]], [[Leonid Levin]], and [[Michael Luby]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Impagliazzo | first1 = Russell | author1-link = Russell Impagliazzo
 | last2 = Levin | first2 = Leonid A. | author2-link = Leonid Levin
 | last3 = Luby | first3 = Michael | author3-link = Michael Luby
 | editor-last = Johnson | editor-first = David S.
 | contribution = Pseudo-random Generation from one-way functions
 | doi = 10.1145/73007.73009
 | pages = 12–24
 | publisher = {ACM}
 | title = Proceedings of the 21st Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, May 14-17, 1989, Seattle, Washington, USA
 | year = 1989| s2cid = 18587852 | doi-access = free}}</ref>

Given a secret [[key (cryptography)|key]] {{mvar|X}} that has {{mvar|n}} [[Discrete uniform distribution|uniform random]] [[bit]]s, of which an [[adversary (cryptography)|adversary]] was able to learn the values of some {{math|''t'' < ''n''}} bits of that key, the leftover hash lemma states that it is possible to produce a key of about {{math|''n'' − ''t''}} bits, over which the adversary has [[almost all|almost no]] knowledge, without knowing which {{math|''t''}} are known to the adversary. Since the adversary knows all but {{math|''n'' − ''t''}} bits, this is almost [[optimal]].

More precisely, the leftover hash lemma states that it is possible to extract a length asymptotic to <math>H_\infty(X)</math> (the [[min-entropy]] of {{mvar|X}}) bits from a [[random variable]] {{mvar|X}}) that are almost uniformly distributed.{{clarify|It's not clear what this sentence states. Please clarify. Also, a parentheses is missing which doesn't help either. And finally, the H_inf notation is NOT what's used for min-entropy in the linked article (it's H_min there).|date=February 2026}} In other words, an adversary who has some partial knowledge about {{mvar|X}}, will have almost no knowledge about the extracted value. This is also known as '''privacy amplification''' (see privacy amplification section in the article [[Quantum key distribution]]).

In quantum cryptographic settings, privacy amplification must also bound information held in a quantum system. Hayashi analyzed the exponential decreasing rate of leaked information for universal random privacy amplification, giving exponent bounds for universal hashing against quantum side information.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hayashi |first=Masahito |date=June 2011 |title=Exponential Decreasing Rate of Leaked Information in Universal Random Privacy Amplification |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=57 |issue=6 |pages=3989-4001 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2011.2110950 |arxiv=0904.0308}}</ref>

[[Randomness extractor]]s achieve the same result, but use (normally) less randomness.

Let {{mvar|X}} be a random variable over <math>\mathcal{X}</math> and let <math>m > 0</math>. Let <math display="inline">h\colon \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \{0,\, 1\}^m</math> be a [[K-independent hashing|2-universal]] [[hash function]]. If 
:<math display="inline">m \leq H_\infty(X) - 2 \log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)</math>
then for {{mvar|S}} uniform over <math>\mathcal{S}</math> and independent of {{mvar|X}}, we have: 
:<math display="inline">\delta\left[(h(S, X), S), (U, S)\right] \leq \varepsilon.</math>

where {{mvar|U}} is uniform over <math>\{0, 1\}^m</math> and independent of {{mvar|S}}.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Rubinfeld | first1 = Ronnit | author1-link = Ronitt Rubinfeld
 | last2 = Drucker | first2 = Andy
 | accessdate = 2019-02-19
 | date = April 30, 2008
 | publisher = MIT
 | title = Lecture 22: The Leftover Hash Lemma and Explicit Extractions
 | url = https://people.csail.mit.edu/ronitt/COURSE/S08/drafts/22.pdf
 | work = Lecture notes for MIT course 6.842, Randomness and Computation}}</ref>

<math display="inline">H_\infty(X) = -\log \max_x \Pr[X=x]</math> is the min-entropy of {{mvar|X}}, which measures the amount of randomness {{mvar|X}} has. The min-entropy is always less than or equal to the [[Shannon entropy]]. Note that <math display="inline">\max_x \Pr[X=x]</math> is the probability of correctly guessing {{mvar|X}}. (The best guess is to guess the most probable value.) Therefore, the min-entropy measures how difficult it is to guess {{mvar|X}}.

<math display="inline">0 \le \delta(X, Y) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_v \left| \Pr[X=v] - \Pr[Y=v] \right| \le 1</math> is a [[statistical distance]] between {{mvar|X}} and {{mvar|Y}}.
